summary: The Confessing Church (Bekennende Kirche) was the movement of German Protestants who, during the 1930s, resisted the Nazi-backed 'German Christian' (Deutsche Christen) movement and the attempt to bring the Protestant churches into line (Gleichschaltung) with National Socialism. Formed around the Pastors' Emergency League of Martin Niemoeller and constituted as a confessing body at the Synod of Barmen (1934), it confessed, in the Barmen Declaration drafted principally by Karl Barth, that the church owes allegiance to Jesus Christ alone and not to the state or any other lord.
description:
The Confessing Church (Bekennende Kirche) was the movement within German Protestantism that arose to resist the alignment of the church with National Socialism during the Kirchenkampf, the German 'church struggle' of the 1930s. After Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933, the pro-Nazi 'German Christian' (Deutsche Christen) movement sought to reorganize the German Evangelical Church along Nazi lines, including the introduction of the so-called Aryan Paragraph, which would have excluded Christians of Jewish descent from church office. In response the Reformed and Lutheran pastors and laity who rejected this program formed, from late 1933, the Pastors' Emergency League (Pfarrernotbund) led by the Berlin pastor Martin Niemoeller, out of which the wider Confessing Church grew.

The movement was constituted as a confessing body at the first Confessing Synod of the German Evangelical Church, held at Barmen (Wuppertal-Barmen) from 29 to 31 May 1934. There it adopted the Theological Declaration of Barmen, drafted principally by the Reformed theologian Karl Barth, which became its founding confessional statement. Barmen's first thesis, prefaced with John 14:6 and John 10, confesses that 'Jesus Christ, as he is attested to us in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God whom we have to hear, and whom we have to trust and obey in life and in death,' and rejects 'the false doctrine that the Church could and should recognize as a source of its proclamation, beyond and besides this one Word of God, yet other events, powers, historic figures and truths as God's revelation.' On this confession the Confessing Church held that the church owes its allegiance to Jesus Christ alone and not to the state, to the Fuehrer, or to the ideology of the age.

The Confessing Church understood itself not as a new denomination but as the true continuation of the German Evangelical Church over against what it regarded as the illegitimate, Nazified official church leadership under the Reich Bishop Ludwig Mueller; it established its own church governing bodies (councils of brethren, Bruderraete) and its own examination and ordination structures, including underground seminaries such as the one Dietrich Bonhoeffer directed at Finkenwalde. It was never a unified political resistance and its members differed over how far opposition should extend, but the movement drew figures including Niemoeller, Barth, and Bonhoeffer. Its members faced surveillance, suppression, arrest, and, in some cases, imprisonment and death: Niemoeller was held for years in concentration camps, Bonhoeffer was executed at Flossenbuerg in April 1945, and a compromised 'official' church structure continued to operate alongside the Confessing Church throughout the period. This entry records the Confessing Church's opposition to the 'German Christian' movement and to the Nazification of the church as the historical stand it was, attributed to the movement, and does not adjudicate the theological disputes internal to German Protestantism.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes the Confessing Church on the tradition's own terms (neutrality #1, #4, #6) and attributes its confessional stand to the movement. Its opposition to the pro-Nazi 'German Christian' movement and to the Gleichschaltung (Nazification) of the Protestant churches is stated as attributed historical fact: the anti-Nazi character of the Confessing Church's resistance is uncontroversial historical record, and it is reported, not editorialized. The intra-Protestant theological disputes (Reformed versus Lutheran, and the differences among Confessing Church members over the extent of opposition) are not adjudicated.

The standard English-language academic study of the Confessing Church, combining archival research with oral histories of more than sixty of its participants; cited as the principal academic-historical lens on the movement's formation, membership, and resistance. Philadelphia: Fortress Press, 1988 (German original 1977). The standard scholarly history of the German church struggle to 1934 by the Tuebingen professor of modern church history, covering the rise of the 'German Christian' movement, the Gleichschaltung of the church, and the road to Barmen; cited as a second academic-historical lens.
